content: The content provided appears to be a highly detailed and technical description of mutations in Mycobacterium tuberculosis and their associations with drug resistance, as well as the methodologies and criteria used for classifying these mutations. Rifampicin resistance mutations also apply to rifapentine. This information is supported by personal communication with Anthony R. in 2023. The second edition of the catalog of mutations in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex and their association with drug resistance provides detailed classifications of mutations, their phenotypic effects, and their sensitivity and specificity in predicting resistance. Mutations in the inhA promoter region, such as -16A>G, -15C>T, -8T>A, and -8T>C, as well as the fabG1 609G>A mutation (Leu203Leu), are known to confer resistance through overexpression of inhA, which is a shared target of isoniazid (INH) and ethionamide (ETO). These mutations are associated with low-level resistance when occurring in isolation but can lead to high-level resistance when combined with other mutations. For example, the inhA Ser94Ala mutation, previously classified in Group 2 for ETO, is now also classified in Group 2 for INH based on transduction experiments. The catalog also highlights the role of katG loss-of-function (LoF) mutations, which are assumed to confer high-level INH resistance. In contrast, in-frame mutations in katG were excluded from additional grading rules in the second edition, as they are less likely to abolish katG function. The WHO-endorsed additional grading rule was applied to classify 128 of the 135 Group 2 mutations, assuming that any katG LoF mutation results in INH resistance. For ethambutol (EMB), 13 non-synonymous mutations in embB and one intergenic mutation upstream of embA met the criteria for Group 1 mutations. However, no Group 2 mutations were identified. The reduced specificity of EMB resistance predictions is likely due to many embB mutations conferring minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) close to the critical concentration (CC), leading to poor agreement with phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (pDST). Regarding pyrazinamide (PZA), only pncA mutations were classified as markers of resistance. Notably, in-frame pncA mutations, such as Gly113_Leu116delinsVal, were excluded from resistance classification due to their lower likelihood of conferring resistance. Intrinsic PZA resistance in Mycobacterium bovis and Mycobacterium canettii is attributed to specific mutations, such as pncA His57Asp in M. bovis. However, the genetic basis of PZA resistance in M. canettii remains unclear. For fluoroquinolones (FQs), significant updates in the second edition include the upgrading of gyrA Asp89Asn and three gyrB mutations (Ser447Phe, Asn499Thr, and Asp461His) to higher confidence groups. All gyrA and gyrB mutations were classified as conferring low-level resistance to moxifloxacin (MFX), except for high-level resistance mutations such as gyrA Gly88Cys and Asp94 variants. Genetically linked low-level resistance mutations may have additive effects, resulting in high-level resistance. For bedaquiline (BDQ) and clofazimine (CFZ), six atpE mutations were classified as Group 2 resistance mutations. Two of these mutations (Ala63Pro and Ile66Met) were identified as arising independently of Rv0678 mutations. The additional grading rule assumes that any LoF mutation in Rv0678 or pepQ confers BDQ resistance. However, the predictive power of Rv0678 mutations may be influenced by epistatic effects, such as the functionality of the corresponding efflux pump. For delamanid (DLM) and pretomanid (PMD), the ddn Leu49Pro mutation remained classified as a Group 2 mutation in the second edition. LoF mutations in other resistance-associated genes (fbiA, fbiB, fbiC, fgd1, and Rv2983) were also recognized as Group 2 mutations based on laboratory experiments. The catalog emphasizes the importance of detecting heteroresistance and rare resistance-conferring mutations. It suggests that revising grading rules will be more informative than including new gene targets in future catalog versions. Additionally, the catalog includes disclaimers for assays that may not account for epistatic effects or novel resistance mechanisms. This transformation maintains the technical depth and specificity of the original content while presenting it in a clear and professional manner suitable for a medical or scientific audience.
